title: Signs and symbols (CCC 1145–1152)
hookLine: water, oil, bread, wine, light: creation speaks

cards: Could a faith get by on ideas alone, with nothing to touch? The Catholic Church doesn't try. At its most solemn moments, it reaches for things any household keeps.
Water poured over a baby's head. Oil traced on a forehead. Bread and wine on an altar.
A candle burning beside a coffin. Holiness, carried by plain stuff. The Catechism's explanation begins where this path went earlier, with body and soul as one person.

teach.b: First, people need signs. Human beings are body and spirit together, the Catechism says, so they take in and express spiritual things through physical ones. A hug says more than a memo.
A ring says something a contract can't. Second, creation already speaks. God talks to people through the visible world: light and darkness, wind and fire, water and earth, the tree and its fruit.
A psalm this path prayed on day one hundred sixty-one says it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands."
So when the Church uses water or light, it isn't inventing a code. It's picking up a language creation was already speaking.

Third, Israel's covenant with God gave these things a history: anointing kings and priests, laying on hands, sacrifice, and above all the Passover. Bread and wine and oil carried memories long before the Church used them.

teach.h: MUD ON A BLIND MAN'S EYES.
teach.b: In John's Gospel he meets a man born blind, spits on the ground, makes a little mud, spreads it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash. The man comes back seeing.
The Catechism says Jesus gave ordinary things a new meaning, and that since Pentecost, the Holy Spirit works through the Church's signs, the sacraments, to make people holy.
So the bread on your counter and the bread on the altar are not the same in Catholic belief. But the one on your counter isn't nothing either. It's part of the same language.

how: In the sacraments Catholics use water in baptism, oil in confirmation and anointing, bread and wine at Mass, and candles at baptisms, funerals and the Easter Vigil.

games.why: he spits on the ground, makes clay, spreads it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash. earth and water, used for healing.

practice: If there's bread nearby, or a glass of water, or anything you'll eat or drink today, hold it and look at it the way you'd look at a gift. Think about where it came from: the field, the rain, the hands that made it and moved it.
If you pray, give thanks before you eat it; if you don't, simply let yourself be grateful, and then eat or drink slowly, as if it meant something.

wordCard.voice: Signs and symbols. Water, oil, bread, wine and light, taken from creation, carried by Israel's covenant, used by Jesus, and in the sacraments, Catholics believe, used by the Spirit. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: creation speaks. The Church didn't invent the language; it picked it up. Until tomorrow.
